profile: FICTIONAL TEST PROFILE. Alex is a software engineer with about four years of experience: two years on a payments backend team (Java, PostgreSQL) and two years building data pipelines and an internal search service (Python, Kafka, Elasticsearch). MS in Computer Science.

stories.title: Shipped a checkout fix before the data was complete
stories.situation: Checkout error rates doubled on a Friday evening after a partner API change. The full logs from the partner would not arrive until Monday.
stories.task: I was on call and had to decide whether to wait for the partner's data or act on partial evidence.
stories.action: I compared our own request logs for the failing calls, found they all used a new currency field, and put the new code path behind a feature flag so I could turn it off for affected currencies only. I told the partner and my manager what I changed and why, and set an alert on the error rate.
stories.result: Checkout errors dropped from about 4% back to 0.3% within an hour. The partner confirmed the root cause on Monday, and the flag let us re-enable the path safely after their fix.
stories.learning: I now write a short rollback plan before acting on partial data, so a fast decision is also a reversible one.

stories.title: Rebuilt a fragile nightly ingestion pipeline
stories.keywords: cron jobs kafka nightly job pipeline simplify
stories.situation: Our search index was fed by three chained nightly cron jobs. When one failed, the index went stale and nobody owned fixing it; it failed about twice a month.
stories.task: It was not formally my team's system, but our search results depended on it, so I proposed owning it.
stories.action: I mapped what each job did, replaced the three jobs with one Kafka consumer that updated the index incrementally, added retries and a dead-letter queue, and wrote a runbook. I did the migration in two phases so the old jobs kept running until the new path matched their output for a week.
stories.result: Index freshness went from up to 24 hours stale to under 5 minutes, and pipeline failures that needed manual action went from about two a month to zero in the following quarter.
stories.learning: Running old and new paths side by side made the migration safe and convinced other teams faster than any design document.

stories.title: Disagreed with a senior engineer about caching
stories.situation: A senior engineer wanted to add a cache in front of the search service to fix slow queries.
stories.task: I thought the slowness came from a few expensive queries, not overall load, and a cache would hide the problem.
stories.action: I pulled a week of query logs and showed that 2% of query patterns caused most of the slow responses. I raised it in our design review with the data, suggested fixing those queries first, and agreed to add the cache later if latency was still high.
stories.result: We optimized the top five query patterns first. p95 latency dropped from 1.8 seconds to 400 milliseconds, and the team decided the cache was not needed yet.
stories.learning: Bringing data and a concrete alternative turned a disagreement into a quick decision.

stories.title: Missed a launch date by underestimating a migration
stories.situation: I committed to moving our payment reconciliation job to a new database in three weeks so finance could close the quarter on the new system.
stories.task: I owned the estimate and the migration.
stories.action: I estimated from the schema size but did not check how many downstream reports read the old tables. In week two I found eleven reports that would break. I told my manager and the finance lead the same day, gave a new date with a list of the reports and an owner for each, and kept the old job running in parallel so finance could still close the quarter.
stories.result: We launched nine days late. Finance closed the quarter on time using the old job, and no report broke after the switch.
stories.learning: I now list every reader of the data before I give a migration estimate, and I share the estimate with its assumptions so people can challenge them.

stories.title: Changed search ranking after reading support tickets
stories.keywords: customer support tickets search ranking complaints
stories.situation: Internal users kept filing support tickets saying search could not find documents they knew existed. The team treated it as user error because our relevance metrics looked fine.
stories.task: I was on the search team and wanted to understand the gap between our metrics and the complaints.
stories.action: I read about 150 tickets and grouped them. Most were searches for exact document IDs and acronyms, which our text analyzer split into pieces. I added an exact-match field and boosted it for ID-shaped queries, and I added those ticket queries to our relevance test set so the metric would catch it next time.
stories.result: Search-related tickets fell from about 40 a month to 6 within two months, and the new test set caught two later regressions before release.
stories.learning: When customer complaints and our metrics disagree, the metric is usually measuring the wrong thing.

turns.question: Given a string s, find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters. For example, for abcabcbb the answer is 3.
turns.review: Understands the task; may ask one clarification or explain the brute force and the sliding-window improvement. Should not dump code yet.

turns.question: Okay, what would the time complexity of your approach be?
turns.review: O(n) with a clear reason (each index enters and leaves the window once); space tied to the character set.

turns.question: Sounds good, go ahead and code it in Python.
turns.review: Explains the approach briefly, then one complete runnable Python solution with line comments.

turns.question: Walk me through a dry run with abcabcbb.
turns.review: Concrete step-by-step window changes with actual indices/characters; ends with 3. No new code proposal.
